strengths: The paper presents a clear and practically relevant motivation: imitation-trained planners can inherit speeding and other undesirable behavior from expert demonstrations.
The two-stage framework is intuitive, combining an autoregressive behavioral prior with reinforcement-learning alignment using interpretable safety, feasibility, and comfort objectives.

The evaluation covers three standard nuPlan splits in both reactive and non-reactive closed-loop settings. Without post-processing, Plan-R1 obtains substantial reactive-score improvements over the strongest reported learning-based baseline, including +5.96 points on Test14-random.

The comparison between the pretrained model and its fine-tuned counterpart shows improvements across collision, TTC, drivable-area, speed, and progress metrics. The KL-weight study and qualitative cases provide additional supporting evidence.
The manuscript is generally well organized, and the dual-model rollout design is explained at a useful conceptual level.
weaknesses: The method is not sufficiently specified for verification or reproduction. The paper defers reward components and implementation details to an appendix, but the supplied manuscript contains no appendix. Reward definitions, weights, safety thresholds, model size, token vocabulary, temporal resolution, GRPO group size, optimizer settings, training budget, sampling parameters, and fine-tuning-data construction are absent.

Equation 5 does not present the standard GRPO clipped surrogate objective and instead uses an unclipped full-trajectory likelihood ratio. It is also unclear how the probability of a joint trajectory containing non-ego actions from a frozen world model is defined under the ego policy. This ambiguity affects the technical soundness of the central optimization method.

The experiments do not establish that GRPO is necessary. There are no comparisons against PPO, REINFORCE, reward-weighted supervised fine-tuning, rejection sampling or best-of-N selection, nor an ablation of individual reward terms or the frozen reactive world model. Consequently, the gains cannot be attributed to the proposed algorithmic choices.

The rule-based rewards closely overlap with nuPlan evaluation criteria. While this can be useful engineering, it weakens the broader claim of general principle alignment. Evaluation is limited to one simulator and benchmark, with no transfer study, unseen-rule evaluation, robustness tests, or analysis of reward exploitation and learned-world-model error.

Results are reported without multiple seeds, confidence intervals, or significance testing. It is also not explicitly stated that the 100,000 fine-tuning scenarios exclude all evaluation scenarios. Several comparisons use externally reported baselines with potentially different implementations and post-processing pipelines.

The pass@k analysis relies on oracle knowledge that at least one sampled trajectory satisfies the criteria, but no mechanism is given for selecting that trajectory at deployment. It therefore does not directly demonstrate operational planning reliability.

Claims such as ensuring safe behavior and suitability for safety-critical planning are stronger than the evidence permits: the method provides no formal safety guarantee and is evaluated only in simulation. Failure modes, computational latency, and ethical or real-world deployment limitations are not discussed.

Overall, the benchmark gains are promising, but limited novelty, an underspecified and possibly inaccurate core objective, missing reproducibility details, and insufficient causal ablations prevent the work from meeting the evidentiary standard of a top-tier acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses an important safety-critical problem and presents an intuitive two-stage framework: autoregressive motion-token pretraining followed by reward-based policy alignment.

The empirical improvements from fine-tuning are meaningful. On Test14-random, the reported score rises from 82.81 to 88.89, with gains in collision, TTC, drivable-area, speed, and progress metrics; reactive results without post-processing also outperform the listed learning-based baselines.
The evaluation includes three nuPlan splits, reactive and non-reactive closed-loop settings, comparisons with numerous planners, qualitative examples, a KL-weight study, and pass@k analysis.
weaknesses: The main technical novelty is limited. Combining an existing motion-token autoregressive architecture with reinforcement learning and standard rule-based nuPlan objectives is relatively incremental, especially given closely related RL-fine-tuned planners such as Gen-Drive and TrajHF. The paper does not isolate what GRPO contributes over PPO, REINFORCE, or other policy-gradient alternatives.

Equation 5 does not present the standard GRPO objective: it omits the clipped surrogate/minimum operation and gives only an unclipped sequence-level likelihood ratio with group-normalized rewards and KL regularization. This is closer to a basic policy-gradient objective than GRPO as normally formulated, making the central methodological characterization questionable.

Reproducibility is poor. Reward definitions and implementation are deferred to an appendix, but the supplied manuscript contains no appendix. It also omits essential architecture dimensions, tokenization settings, reward weights, safety thresholds, GRPO group size, optimization hyperparameters, training schedule, sampling procedure, inference policy, and computational cost.

The frozen learned predictor is treated as a reactive world model during RL without evidence that it remains reliable under ego actions that depart from the demonstration distribution. This creates a substantial risk of model exploitation or reward hacking; no world-model accuracy, out-of-distribution, or simulator-transfer analysis is provided.

The evaluation does not establish whether improvements come specifically from the proposed algorithm. The only central ablation is fine-tuned versus non-fine-tuned, with no comparisons among individual rewards, alternative RL algorithms, direct supervised/rule-based fine-tuning, the dual-model design, or training without the learned world model.

Reported results lack uncertainty estimates, repeated seeds, or significance tests. This matters for closed-loop simulation scores and hyperparameter-selected results. The pass@k analysis likewise gives no sample count or confidence intervals and has limited relevance unless a practical mechanism can safely select the successful trajectory.

The state-of-the-art language is overstated. With post-processing, Plan-R1 is worse than Diffusion Planner on Test14-hard in both non-reactive and reactive modes and worse on Test14-random non-reactive evaluation. Comparisons are also confounded by an external refinement module whose implementation and interaction with Plan-R1 are not described.

The paper generalizes simulator benchmark gains into broad claims of safe and feasible planning without robustness tests, rare-event evaluation, real-world validation, or discussion of failure cases and limitations. For a safety-critical application, this evidentiary gap is important. strengths: The paper identifies an important practical problem: imitation-learned planners can inherit unsafe behavior from imperfect demonstrations, and explicit post-training alignment is a sensible response.
Plan-R1 presents a clear and coherent two-stage framework combining autoregressive motion-token pretraining with rule-guided reinforcement learning.

The benchmark coverage is reasonably broad within nuPlan, spanning three established splits and both reactive and non-reactive closed-loop evaluation. Comparisons include strong learning-based, rule-based, and hybrid planners.

The reported reactive results are promising. Without post-processing, Plan-R1 improves over Diffusion Planner by 2.17, 3.96, and 5.96 points on the three reactive splits. The direct ablation reports a 6.08-point aggregate gain from fine-tuning, with improvements in collision, TTC, drivable-area, speed, and progress metrics.
The rule-based objectives are interpretable, and the qualitative examples clearly illustrate correction of speeding, off-road driving, and collision behavior.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is substantially inadequate. The manuscript refers readers to an appendix for reward and implementation details, but the supplied paper has no appendix. It omits the precise reward definitions and weights, tokenization parameters, model dimensions, GRPO group size, optimization settings, training schedule, compute requirements, and other essential hyperparameters.

The fine-tuning benefit is established only against pretraining without fine-tuning. There is no comparison with PPO, REINFORCE, best-of-N or reward-based selection, constrained decoding, or another RL objective, so the evidence does not establish that GRPO is important rather than rule-based optimization generally.

The individual reward components are not ablated. Consequently, it is unclear which principles drive the gains, whether multiplicative safety indicators are necessary, or how sensitive performance is to reward weights. Only the KL coefficient receives a sensitivity study.

The presentation of GRPO is technically incomplete: Equation 5 omits the clipped surrogate central to standard GRPO/PPO-style optimization and does not clearly explain how ego-token likelihood ratios and KL penalties are computed when trajectories also contain samples from the frozen agent model.

Evaluation optimizes and measures closely overlapping rule-based criteria, creating some circularity. There are no evaluations on a second simulator or dataset, rare safety-critical subsets, distribution shifts, or learned/reactive traffic agents beyond IDM. Thus, claims about general safety and real-world feasibility are stronger than the evidence.

No variance across seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported, making it difficult to assess the robustness of the moderate score differences. The pass@k plot likewise lacks uncertainty and detailed sample counts.

The state-of-the-art claim is overstated. Plan-R1 does not lead every split or setting: for example, with post-processing it trails Diffusion Planner on Test14-hard reactive evaluation, and without post-processing it is not consistently best in non-reactive evaluation.

The conceptual novelty is moderate rather than major: autoregressive motion tokenization, rule-based planning rewards, and RL fine-tuning are individually established, with closely related contemporaneous approaches acknowledged. The paper needs stronger algorithmic comparisons and analysis to demonstrate that their particular combination constitutes a top-tier contribution.

Given the safety-critical application, the paper should explicitly discuss simulator-to-real limitations, reward misspecification, failure modes, and the absence of deployment-level safety guarantees.

strengths: Addresses an important safety-critical planning problem with an intuitive two-stage design: imitation pretraining supplies realistic behavior, while rule-based RL explicitly targets safety, comfort, progress, and traffic compliance.
The dual-model rollout is practically motivated and enables interaction-aware fine-tuning without updating the surrounding-agent model.

Results on multiple standard nuPlan splits are strong, especially in reactive evaluation; the learning-only model substantially improves over the pretrained baseline and outperforms prior learning-based planners on reactive closed-loop scores.
The paper includes useful ablations covering GRPO versus VD-GRPO, reward components, group size, KL/scaling hyperparameters, model capacity, and reactive versus replayed surrounding agents.
The advantage-distribution and unsafe-group analyses provide plausible empirical support for the claimed failure mode of per-group variance normalization.
The presentation is generally clear, and the appendix reports architecture, training resources, principal hyperparameters, and reward weights.
weaknesses: The algorithmic novelty is limited: VD-GRPO primarily removes per-group standard-deviation normalization and adds a fixed scale, closely resembling the cited Dr.GRPO modification. There is no direct comparison with Dr.GRPO or other normalization/clipping alternatives to establish a distinct contribution.

The RL objective is underspecified and appears not to contain the clipped surrogate normally central to GRPO/PPO. Important details such as exact KL estimation and whether clipping is used in implementation are absent, making the method difficult to assess and reproduce.

The manuscript contradicts Equation 5 when discussing the scaling constant: because rewards are divided by c, increasing c reduces rather than amplifies the RL gradient. More broadly, c changes the effective RL learning rate and its balance against KL regularization, so the claimed safety-specific benefit is not cleanly separated from optimization-scale tuning.

Evaluation is limited to one benchmark and rewards largely optimize the same rule-based quantities used by the nuPlan score. This leaves open benchmark-reward overfitting and does not substantiate broad claims about real-world safety or generalization to genuinely challenging interactions.
No uncertainty estimates, repeated-seed results, or significance tests are provided. This matters for the smaller GRPO-to-VD-GRPO gains and safety-metric changes.

The split used for ablations and hyperparameter selection is not stated. The full-model values in Tables 2–5 match Test14-random, raising concern that beta, c, group size, and reward design may have been selected or analyzed on a test split.

The reactive world model is not evaluated for predictive accuracy, calibration, or realism under ego-policy distribution shift. The dual-model ablation shows a score benefit but does not establish that learned reactions are realistic; its capacity comparison is also confounded because the doubled pretrained model does not receive equivalent RL fine-tuning.

Several claims are overstated: hand-designed rewards and weights are not inherently unbiased, IDM-based reactive simulation is only a limited proxy for realistic behavior, and Plan-R1 is not uniformly state of the art across all reported settings.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: safety and comfort thresholds, overspeed normalization threshold, sampling settings for pass@k, preprocessing/map encoding, scenario-selection procedure, and code are not provided. The pass@k study also lacks a deployable sample-selection mechanism and conflicts with the stated top-1 inference protocol.

strengths: The paper identifies an important practical problem: imitation-learned planners can reproduce unsafe or undesirable behavior present in demonstrations.
The two-stage design is intuitive, and using a frozen predictor for interactive fine-tuning is a plausible way to retain realistic behavior while optimizing explicit objectives.

The reported closed-loop improvements are substantial in reactive nuPlan evaluation; the unrefined model improves R-CLS over Diffusion Planner by 4.89, 7.98, and 7.11 points on Val14, Test14-hard, and Test14-random, respectively.
The paper includes useful ablations covering GRPO versus VD-GRPO, reward components, group size, scaling, KL regularization, model capacity, and world-model choice.
weaknesses: The central VD-GRPO method has limited novelty: removing within-group standard-deviation normalization closely resembles the cited Dr.GRPO. The fixed constant chiefly rescales the policy-gradient term relative to the learning rate and KL penalty, and the paper does not clearly establish a distinct algorithmic contribution.

The optimizer study omits crucial baselines, especially Dr.GRPO, PPO, DAPO, and globally normalized or batch-normalized returns. Comparing only standard GRPO with the proposed variant does not show that VD-GRPO is preferable to existing alternatives or even to simpler rescaling strategies.

Evaluation is strongly aligned with the training reward: collision, drivable-area compliance, speed, comfort, TTC, and progress are both optimized during fine-tuning and used to construct the nuPlan score. Without independent safety tests, distribution shifts, adversarial cases, or a separate evaluation simulator, the results may largely demonstrate benchmark-metric optimization.

The safety claims are too strong for evidence from one simulator benchmark. No real-world evaluation, out-of-domain testing, rare-event stress testing, uncertainty analysis, or raw collision counts are provided. Aggregate scores near saturation obscure the practical frequency and severity of failures.

There are no multiple-seed results, confidence intervals, or significance tests. This is particularly problematic for RL fine-tuning and for comparatively small ablation differences, such as the 1.69-point R-CLS gain of VD-GRPO over GRPO.

The learned reactive world model is asserted to be realistic but its prediction accuracy, calibration, closed-loop drift, and failure modes are never evaluated. Training uses this learned model whereas reactive evaluation uses IDM, leaving unclear whether improvements reflect robust interaction learning or simulator-specific artifacts.

The dual-model ablation is overinterpreted. The direct comparison between GT replay and the reactive world model is 87.44 versus 90.04 R-CLS, while the claimed 7.23-point benefit conflates the world model with the entire RL fine-tuning procedure.

Several claims are insufficiently justified: rule-based rewards are described as unbiased despite embedding hand-selected metrics and weights; high reward variance is treated as synonymous with safety criticality; and the advantage-distribution plots provide correlation rather than causal evidence for the proposed explanation.

Reproducibility is incomplete: important reward thresholds, rollout and policy-update details, token construction choices, and the exact GRPO objective implementation are missing. Equation 4 also lacks the clipping operation normally central to GRPO/PPO-style optimization, making the implemented algorithm ambiguous.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: correcting unsafe or undesirable behaviors inherited from human driving demonstrations while retaining useful behavioral priors.
Plan-R1 is conceptually clear and practically motivated. The separation between autoregressive pre-training, rule-based RL alignment, and a frozen reactive agent model forms a coherent framework.

The empirical results are strong. Without post-processing, Plan-R1 substantially improves reactive closed-loop scores over Diffusion Planner on Val14, Test14-hard, and Test14-random; the gains on the hard reactive split are particularly compelling.
The evaluation includes competitive learning-based, rule-based, and hybrid baselines across standard nuPlan splits in both reactive and non-reactive settings.

The ablations cover the main components, including GRPO versus VD-GRPO, reactive-world-model versus logged-trajectory rollouts, model capacity, group size, reward components, KL weight, scaling constant, and pass@k behavior.

VD-GRPO is well motivated by an empirical analysis of advantage distributions. The reported recovery in collision avoidance relative to standard GRPO supports the central claim that per-group variance normalization can dilute rare safety signals.
The paper is clearly organized, visually polished, and provides useful architecture, optimization, compute, and reward-design details.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is moderate. The overall pre-training-plus-RL recipe follows established alignment and driving approaches, while removing group standard-deviation normalization is closely related to Dr.GRPO. The main novelty is therefore the safety-planning interpretation and integration rather than a fundamentally new optimization algorithm.

The evidence is based only on nuPlan and its simulator metrics. There is no cross-dataset, real-world, or substantially out-of-distribution evaluation, limiting support for broad claims of safe and robust trajectory planning.

No uncertainty estimates, confidence intervals, or multi-seed results are reported. This is important because RL fine-tuning and relatively small score differences, such as VD-GRPO versus GRPO, may be sensitive to randomness and checkpoint selection.

The learned world model is trained from observational demonstrations but used for counterfactual reactions to exploratory ego actions. Its reaction accuracy or calibration under such off-distribution interventions is not directly evaluated.

The dual-model ablation only partially isolates the claimed benefit. The appropriate comparison indicates a 2.60-point gain from replacing ground-truth replay with the reactive model, whereas the larger 7.23-point improvement cited in the discussion also includes the effect of RL fine-tuning.

Several central descriptions are underspecified for exact reproduction, including token-clustering settings, sampling details during RL, safety thresholds, clipping behavior in the GRPO objective, and some reward implementation constants.

The claim that rule-based rewards are consistent and unbiased is too strong: reward definitions, weights, thresholds, simulator dynamics, and the expert-normalized progress term all encode design choices and potential biases.

The appendix contains an internal mathematical contradiction: since rewards are divided by the scaling constant c, increasing c weakens rather than amplifies the RL gradients, contrary to one part of the stated interpretation. More generally, VD-GRPO lacks a formal analysis of when variance correlates with safety violations or guarantees safety-priority preservation.

The safety evidence remains benchmark-relative rather than a safety guarantee. Aggregate closed-loop scores and selected qualitative cases do not characterize rare-event performance, severity-conditioned failures, or the possibility of reward exploitation.
